query: Casting is the predominant fabrication method for high-entropy alloys, but solidification-related porosity and microstructural nonuniformity can cause heterogeneous properties. Studies of other high-entropy-alloy compositions have reported high hardness and notable compressive performance, yet these findings do not establish how to improve CoCrFeNiTi; moreover, some investigated alloys were brittle at 25 °C and displayed only limited plastic deformation at 600 °C. For equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with a simple crystal structure, favorable plasticity and machinability, but low hardness and load-bearing capability, what single intervention could improve hardness and mechanical performance while preserving those favorable characteristics and clarifying the relationship between microstructure and deformation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, a quantitative prediction relative to the unmodified alloy, the processing and testing boundaries within which it should apply, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled microstructural and mechanical experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of titanium to the CoCrFeNiTi alloy will improve its hardness and mechanical performance while preserving its favorable plasticity and machinability.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with a simple crystal structure
generation.intervention: Addition of a small amount of titanium
generation.conditions: Room temperature and standard atmospheric conditions
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a solid solution with a face-centered cubic (fcc) or body-centered cubic (bcc) structure
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening and solid solution strengthening
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved hardness and mechanical performance, including increased yield strength and toughness
generation.boundary: The alloy's microstructure and mechanical properties will be affected by the addition of titanium, but the exact boundaries of this effect are unknown
generation.uncertainty: The optimal amount of titanium to add and the exact mechanisms by which it improves the alloy's properties are unknown

falsification_experiment.design: A controlled experiment in which the CoCrFeNiTi alloy is modified with different amounts of titanium and its microstructure and mechanical properties are measured
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of titanium does not improve the alloy's hardness and mechanical performance, the hypothesis is falsified

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. The requirements for designing novel metallic alloys that are capable of surpassing a whole set of specific properties of currently available commercial alloys are, at present, a subject of high demand in the industry. For instance, an improved combination of metallic alloys should possess strength and ductility while maintaining a relatively low cost. This is especially true when one is dealing with materials for high-temperature applications. Therefore, new engineering solutions are needed for novel materials that outperform the capabilities of the currently used Ni-based alloys. One of the prospective innovative materials that could be able to meet the requirements of such demanding applications, especially in the aviation and aerospace industries, may be refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). These are also known by other names, such as complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). These materials have been extensively studied in recent years [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] due to their very interesting combination of properties in some of the compositions.
